title: The Crusades, honestly
hook: armed pilgrimages that included massacres in Jerusalem and attacks on Jewish communities

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hildegard and viriditas, the life God gives. Your line was the green life. Today's story is harder, and it asks for honesty.

A piece of cloth, cut in the shape of a cross, sewn onto a tunic at the shoulder. In the accounts of that day, a pope has just finished preaching to a crowd in France, and people are pressing forward to vow that they'll go east. Farmers, knights, priests. Some will walk all the way to Jerusalem. They think of themselves as pilgrims. They are also an army. The word crusade holds both of those at once, and today asks us not to drop either half.
screen: `A CLOTH CROSS AT THE SHOULDER.` → `PILGRIMS, AND AN ARMY.` → `HOLD BOTH HALVES.`

segments.voice: Pope Urban the Second urged Western Christians to go east, to help Christians there and to reach Jerusalem. The accounts that survive disagree about his exact words. Those who answered took a vow and marked themselves with the cross. So a crusade was an armed pilgrimage: prayer and penance, joined to war. Before they even left Europe, bands of crusaders turned on Jewish communities in towns along the Rhine. Jewish chronicles from those towns remember the dead, and families who chose death over forced baptism. Some bishops sheltered Jewish families; some could not stop the killing. When the crusaders took Jerusalem, they killed its people, Muslims and Jews, in the streets and in holy places. A Christian chronicler who was there describes the slaughter without shame. There were voices from inside the Church too. When a monk later stirred up attacks on Jews during another crusade, Bernard of Clairvaux wrote that the Jews were not to be persecuted, and went in person to silence him. And in a jubilee year, Pope John Paul the Second led the Church in asking God's forgiveness for violence used in the service of the truth, and for sins against the people of Israel. Telling it honestly means keeping both halves: the faith that made people walk so far, and the crimes some of them committed on the way.
screen: `AN ARMED PILGRIMAGE.` · `ATTACKS ALONG THE RHINE.` · `SLAUGHTER IN JERUSALEM.` · `VOICES OF SORROW AND PARDON.` · then, large: `TELL IT HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Hold the Holy Land in mind, its hills and old stone streets, and the people who live there now, of every faith, and those grieving there today, without taking a side. If you pray, the Douay-Rheims psalm gives you the words: pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem. If you don't, hold them with a wish for their safety.
Crusade. An armed pilgrimage under the sign of the cross, joining prayer and penance to war, and carrying both faith and grave crimes. Today's word.
Your line: tell it honestly. Both halves belong in the telling. That's day eight hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for peace in the Holy Land at Mass and in parish intentions, and the Church's own acts of repentance, like the Day of Pardon in the jubilee year, name the violence of the past alongside its faith.

chat.says: Were the Crusades holy pilgrimages or just wars? Which was it?
options: Both: armed pilgrimages of real faith, which also brought grave crimes, told honestly.
Just wars: nobody who went had any real faith; it was all about land.
Just pilgrimages: the killing was invented much later by the Church's critics.
chat.meaning: A crusade joined prayer and penance to war. Telling it honestly keeps both halves: the faith, and the crimes some crusaders committed on the way.

notes: Sensitive day: please check tone toward Jewish and Muslim listeners and Catholic listeners alike. No numbers of dead are given under the claims rule.
Urban II at Clermont: accounts differ (Fulcher, Robert the Monk, Baldric, Guibert); the cloth cross at the shoulder is from these accounts. Confirm.

Rhineland: 'some bishops sheltered Jewish families' (e.g., Bishop John of Speyer); 'some could not stop the killing' (e.g., Mainz). Hebrew chronicles record martyrdom rather than forced baptism. Confirm wording.
Jerusalem: a Christian eyewitness (Raymond of Aguilers; also the Gesta Francorum) describes the killing in the Temple area without shame. Confirm.

Bernard's letter (Ep. 363 and to the archbishop of Mainz) and his going to silence the monk Radulf, during the Second Crusade. Bernard also preached that crusade; the script does not hide this but doesn't develop it. Keeper may want it named.
Day of Pardon (March 12, 2000; year kept out of the voice): confessions of 'sins committed in the service of truth' and 'sins against the people of Israel'. Confirm wording.
Day 777 (1204) covered the sack of Constantinople; this day deliberately leaves it out to avoid repeating that angle.
Audit pass: match pair said John Paul II 'asked forgiveness for that violence'; the Day of Pardon confesses violence in the service of truth without naming the crusades, so the pair now says that.
